# Canals and pound locks (`canal_locks`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation, hydraulic_cement
- Core idea: A pound lock is a chamber with a gate at each end: the boat enters, the gate behind it closes, sluices let water in or out until the level matches the next stretch, the gate ahead opens. Water moves from the upper reach to the lower one in a lock cycle. A summit reach needs a reliable supply, supplied by streams, reservoirs or pumps. Mitre gates, two leaves meeting at an angle pointing upstream, are pressed shut by the water itself. A horse that can pull about 1 tonne on a road tows 30 tonnes or more in a canal boat.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting the summit water supply; many canals failed because they ran dry in summer
  - Gates pointing downstream, which the water pushes open
  - Crediting Leonardo with inventing the lock; pound locks existed in Milan decades before him (his mitre-gate design is real but its first use is disputed)
- History: china: 214 BC – Lingqu canal with navigation weirs; 605–610 Sui Grand Canal; 984 Qiao Weiyue's pound lock on the Grand Canal; europe: 1373 – chamber lock at Vreeswijk (Netherlands); 1438–39 original Conca di Viarenna, Milan (rebuilt at a different site in the 16th c.); 1497 Martesana connected to Milan's inner canal ring; c. 1500 Leonardo's mitre gates; 1681 Canal du Midi; 1761 Bridgewater Canal
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 3: Civil Engineering and Nautics (1971)
  - Charles Hadfield, World Canals: Inland Navigation Past and Present (1986)
